accuracy.evidence: Every solid in the lab is built from real geometry: the cube mesh has 6 congruent square faces, the cuboid is 3.1 by 1.5 by 1.5 so its long faces are rectangles, the square-based pyramid has 4 triangular faces meeting at an apex, the cylinder has 2 circular flat faces and 1 curved surface, the cone 1 circular flat face, 1 curved surface and an apex, and the sphere is curved everywhere. The print step matches flat faces to their 2-D shapes (pyramid side = triangle, cylinder end = circle, cuboid side = long rectangle). 6-n, 2*n, n and t give whole answers at every corner. The K.G.A.1-3 and Year 1 wording matches the published standards, and the adult text notes that curved surfaces are not called faces in Year 2 work.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-geometry errors: naming a solid by a 2-D name (a ball is a circle, a dice is a square, a box is a rectangle), cube vs cuboid, cone vs pyramid or triangle because of the side view, counting only the 3 visible faces of a cube, and believing round solids have no flat face. Each appears as a distractor in the name, print or home rounds and in the Challenge.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsolid renders real rotatable 3-D meshes with back-face culling: the child drags to turn a cube to reach hidden faces, taps faces on the turning solid, and matches paint prints to the solid's flat face. No other flag lab turns a solid in 3-D; Building towers and bridges (flagtower) is about stacking and balance, and Circles, squares and triangles (flagshape) is about flat shapes. The 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child cannot finish step 1 without turning the cube, so they find out that 3 faces are always hidden; step 2 makes them tap the top, side and bottom of a cylinder and then a cone, so flat face and curved surface are felt before they are named; the print step shows that a flat face of a solid is a flat shape and a sphere has none; the home step links the names to a tin, ball, dice, box and party hat.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 3 faces for a cube (what you can see), 0 flat faces for a cylinder (it is round), and a cone printing a triangle (its side view). The lab then disproves each and the completion line repeats the learner's guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions; every wrong option has its own message: cuboid vs cube, flat name for a solid, a ball as a cylinder, round solids with no flat face, a cylinder with 1 face, a cone's flat face as a triangle, counting only the seen faces, guessing 4, cone vs pyramid and a cube's lack of a point. Option order rotates.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences about holding, turning and counting (readability check within the 6.5 limit); lab prompts are under fifteen words with big 56 px buttons. Adult notes stay within 9.5 and use the precise terms 3-D shape, face, curved surface, cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone, pyramid and congruent.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid sentence is a fact or an action; the adult paragraphs are a standards reference, vocabulary notes, a list of named mistakes and what each lab step does. The family tip is a kitchen solid hunt with a flour print and a question. The filler scan found nothing.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark: the solid fills the canvas without clipping, face labels sit in pills only on faces that face the viewer, answer tiles with mini solids and names fit three across at 390 px, and every control is a 56 px young-layout button under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (Turn left, Turn right, Tip up, Tip down, Tap the front part), names and solids are buttons, the canvas aria-label updates with each spoken line (faces found, flat or curved), and the walkthrough's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
